newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition hails victory as watershed.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition hails victory as watershed.

text.p: Serbia's opposition said on Monday they scored a "historic" victory in the capital Belgrade and major towns across the country in weekend local elections.
Thousands of people crammed into the capital's Republic Square to celebrate the results at an opposition rally.
"Good afternoon free Belgrade, good afternoon free Serbia. Zoran Djindjic, leader of the opposition Democratic Party, told the rally.
"Are you already breathing easier?" he asked, drawing a roar from the crowd.
The Democratic Party ran in the elections as part of the Zajedno (Together) coalition with the Serbian Renewal Movement and the Civic Alliance
The opposition leaders appeared suprised by the scale of their victory against the ruling leftist coalition of Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic.
Even as they celebrated, opposition leaders expressed fears the "regime" might try to steal votes and reverse the results.
After the rally, the crowd marched to the city hall, where opposition leaders met the head of the Belgrade electoral commission, Dragomir Lazarevic.
While the crowd chanted outside the building, leaders of the opposition coalition held a tense discussion with Lazarevic as reporters looked on.
"We would not like the clearly expressed wish of the citizens to be forged in the end," Vuk Draskovic, head of the Serbian Renewal Movement, told the official.
Lazarevic replied: "As for the verification of the electoral results -- until the moment the city electoral commission declares them publicly -- nobody has won."

The municipal polls came two weeks after Milosevic's coalition scored a resounding victory in national elections -- its first big electoral test since the end of four years of war in former Yugoslavia.
But ruling Socialist party officials effectively conceded defeat in major towns in the municipal voting.
Ivica Dacic, spokesman for the Socialist Party of Serbia, said the leftist coalition won in 134 municipalities out of 174 in Serbia. But none of the big towns were on his list.
"The left (Milosevic's) coalition has 25 out of 110 councillors in the Belgrade city assembly," he said.
Loss of control of the capital's city assembly would be a blow to Milosevic and sources close to the government said Socialist leaders were "shattered" by the election results.
Analysts said national power would remain with Milosevic, who keeps a tight grip on the police, media and finances.
But the result was an unprecedented electoral embarassment, threatening Milosevic's aura of invincibility.

By winning control of major municipalities, the opposition could make life difficult for Milosevic in the months leading up to crucial elections in the Serbian republic sometime next year, analysts said.

In Sunday's municipal run-off -- covering 5,603 city council seats in municipalities where no candidate had managed to obtain a majority in the first round -- the opposition claimed victory in the 12 biggest Serbian towns.
Apart from Belgrade, the towns included major industrial centres such as Nis, Kragujevac, Uzice, Kraljevo, Kikinda, Zrenjanin and Cacak, and Novi Sad, the provincial capital of Vojvodina.

In Belgrade a Democratic Party spokesman, quoting incomplete results, said Zajedno had won 70 seats, the Socialist Party of Serbia 23, the ultra-nationalist Radical Party 15, and the right-wing Democratic Party of Serbia two.
Opposition supporters were ecstatic over the victory and said Milosevic's nine-year rule was now in jeopardy.
"I heard the results this moring and I couldn't believe it," said Nadezda Krzic, a middle-aged woman attending the Zajedno rally. "Maybe this is the beginning of the end."
